paragraphs: Learning in a game can produce complicated behavior because each player's updates interact with everyone else's. This paper studies that behavior by separating games into components with more understandable dynamics. It draws inspiration from a decomposition of vector fields into potential and incompressible parts, but argues that the usual Euclidean geometry does not fit exponential, or multiplicative, weights learning.

The authors instead use a Riemannian geometry based on the Shahshahani metric and define incompressible games within that framework. For these games, they prove that continuous-time exponential weights dynamics preserve volume and possess a quantity that remains constant along trajectories. They also establish Poincaré recurrence: almost every trajectory returns arbitrarily close to its initial position infinitely often.

The paper then connects this dynamical classification to an existing decomposition into potential and harmonic games. It proves that incompressibility and harmonicity are equivalent. Consequently, the recurrence result applies to harmonic games as well, providing a precise explanation of persistent revisiting behavior for this class under continuous-time exponential weights.
icml-2024-a-geometric-decomposition-of-f.tldr: A geometry adapted to exponential weights reveals that continuous-time learning in harmonic games returns near its starting point infinitely often for almost every trajectory.

paragraphs: Music language models often work with audio tokens produced by an autoencoder using several codebooks. Predicting these token streams creates a tradeoff. Modeling their full joint distribution requires more sequential prediction steps, while modeling each codebook's marginal distribution separately is an imperfect approximation unless the codebooks are mutually independent.

This paper addresses that tradeoff by changing how the audio tokenizer is trained. It introduces an additional loss that encourages independence between codebooks. The loss uses maximum mean discrepancy in a kernel-based function space as a proxy for mutual information. Its purpose is to make separate predictions across codebooks better match the statistical structure of the tokens themselves.

The authors show that the loss reduces dependence between codebooks during autoencoding. When the music model uses a product of marginal distributions, this change improves generated music quality while retaining much faster audio generation than the joint-distribution model. The contribution therefore links tokenizer design to generation efficiency, and the proposed criterion can also extend to other codecs with multiple streams.
icml-2024-an-independence-promoting-loss.tldr: Encouraging independence between audio codebooks improves music generation with separate token-stream predictions while retaining their speed advantage over joint modeling.

paragraphs: Continual test-time adaptation updates a model during deployment as its environment changes. The challenge is both computational and statistical: updates must be efficient, and learning a new domain should preserve useful capabilities for domains that may return later. BECoTTA addresses these requirements with an input-dependent collection of specialized experts.

Its central component, Mixture-of-Domain Low-rank Experts, combines domain-adaptive routing with a domain-expert synergy loss. The routing helps select knowledge suited to the current input's domain. The loss encourages stronger dependence between domains and experts, supporting specialization within the collection. Low-rank experts make this adaptation framework economical in trainable parameters and memory.

Across multiple continual adaptation benchmarks, the authors report a 5.81% performance gain while requiring 0.001 times the trainable parameters in their reported comparison. They also examine how inputs are assigned to experts and how target domains relate to one another. These findings support the approach as a way to combine selective adaptation with low parameter cost under changing deployment conditions.
icml-2024-becotta-input-dependent-online.tldr: BECoTTA uses domain-aware routing among low-rank experts to improve continual test-time adaptation with very few trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Cell2Sentence adapts language models to single-cell transcriptomics by converting gene expression measurements into sequences called cell sentences. This representation gives biological data a form that language models can use directly during fine-tuning. The central idea is to connect existing language-model machinery with tasks involving the molecular characteristics of individual cells.

The authors demonstrate this approach on several tasks, including generating cell representations, assigning complex cell-type labels, and producing text directly from biological data. In their experiments, GPT-2 fine-tuned with Cell2Sentence generates biologically valid cells when given cell-type inputs and accurately predicts cell types from cell sentences. These are complementary uses of the same biological representation.

The findings suggest that this fine-tuning approach can teach a language model substantial information about single-cell biology while preserving strong text generation abilities. Its practical appeal is the ability to use existing models and libraries for biological applications. The paper therefore presents a flexible representation framework that connects biological prediction and generation with natural-language capabilities.
icml-2024-cell2sentence-teaching-large-l.tldr: Cell2Sentence turns gene expression data into sequences that let language models learn cell-type prediction, cell generation, and biology-related text generation.

paragraphs: Object completion seeks to reconstruct an entire object when only some of it is visible. MaskComp approaches this task by repeatedly connecting image generation with segmentation. The object mask provides shape information for generation, while segmentation extracts shape information from the generated images. Each stage therefore produces information that can improve the next.

In each iteration, the current object mask becomes an additional condition for generating images. The method then combines segmentations of those images to obtain a more accurate mask. The authors demonstrate that one generation stage followed by one segmentation stage effectively acts as a mask denoiser, refining the shape information available to the process.

Repeating this cycle progressively improves the partial object mask and gives generation more precise guidance about the complete object's shape. Experiments show better object completion than the evaluated existing approaches, including ControlNet and Stable Diffusion. The contribution is the feedback between generating appearance and estimating shape: the two operations cooperate throughout reconstruction instead of serving as isolated steps.
icml-2024-completing-visual-objects-via-.tldr: MaskComp alternates image generation and segmentation to refine partial object masks and improve reconstruction of complete objects.

paragraphs: Optimization with Riemannian constraints requires updates that respect the geometry of the feasible space. Computing the required gradients and retractions exactly can be costly. This paper asks when cheaper, approximate computations still allow Riemannian gradient descent to converge, and how many iterations are needed in general nonconvex, constrained problems.

The authors analyze these questions through tangential Block Majorization-Minimization, or tBMM. They establish convergence to an epsilon-stationary point within O(epsilon^-2) iterations. This is a guarantee of approximate stationarity, rather than a claim of reaching a global optimum. Under a mild assumption, the guarantee also holds with inexact subproblem solutions when the total optimality gap is bounded.

The framework covers several established methods, including inexact Riemannian gradient descent and proximal gradient methods on Stiefel manifolds. Numerical evaluations report improved performance on constrained tensor decomposition, regularized nonnegative matrix factorization, and low-rank matrix recovery. Together, the analysis and experiments support using controlled approximation to make geometric optimization more practical while retaining stated convergence guarantees.
icml-2024-convergence-and-complexity-gua.tldr: A general optimization framework provides convergence guarantees for Riemannian methods that use cheaper, controlled approximations.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through a continuous sampling process, yet particular features can emerge during surprisingly narrow intervals. This paper calls those intervals critical windows. Understanding them could make generation easier to interpret by connecting an output property, such as image class or background color, to a specific portion of the sampling trajectory.

The authors develop a formal framework and prove bounds on these windows for data drawn from mixtures of strongly log-concave densities. The bounds depend on measures of separation between groups and within groups. They also work out concrete examples involving well-conditioned Gaussian mixtures, connecting the general theory to distributions with explicit structure.

These results support a rigorous interpretation of diffusion models as hierarchical samplers that progressively settle output features at a discrete sequence of times. Experiments on synthetic data validate the bounds. The authors also show that critical windows may help diagnose fairness and privacy violations in real-world diffusion models, extending their possible usefulness beyond understanding when image features emerge.
icml-2024-critical-windows-non-asymptoti.tldr: Under structured mixture assumptions, the paper bounds narrow sampling intervals when diffusion-model features emerge and interprets generation as hierarchical decision-making.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction sets to express uncertainty and offers theoretical guarantees through a model-agnostic, distribution-free framework. This paper studies a distinct security question: whether an adversary can poison data to manipulate the uncertainty reported for particular examples. The target is the uncertainty result itself, rather than simply causing an incorrect class prediction.

The authors introduce a class of black-box poisoning attacks designed around this objective and develop optimization frameworks for carrying them out. They evaluate the attacks in several settings, including full and split conformal prediction. This places the evaluation directly on the behavior of uncertainty estimation under deliberately corrupted data.

In the reported experiments, these dedicated attacks manipulate uncertainty more effectively than conventional poisoning attacks aimed at misclassification. Existing defenses against conventional attacks are also ineffective against the proposed attacks in the evaluations. The findings show why uncertainty systems merit their own adversarial analysis: an attack objective centered on prediction sets can expose weaknesses that classification-oriented attacks and defenses do not adequately address.
icml-2024-data-poisoning-attacks-against.tldr: Dedicated black-box poisoning attacks manipulate conformal prediction uncertainty more effectively than misclassification-focused attacks in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: DARL explores whether predicting image content can also teach a model useful visual representations. It uses a decoder-only Transformer to predict image patches autoregressively, with each prediction made in sequence. The authors first find that training this architecture with mean squared error alone produces strong representations, making a simple generative objective a useful starting point.

To improve image generation, they replace that loss with a diffusion objective implemented through a denoising patch decoder. They then study how the noise schedule and training affect representation quality. Tailored schedules and longer training in larger models improve the learned representations, and the best schedule differs substantially from schedules typically used in standard image diffusion models.

Under a fine-tuning evaluation protocol, DARL performs close to leading masked prediction models despite its simple architecture. The findings support combining autoregressive prediction with denoising as a route toward models that serve both visual perception and generation. They also show that choices suited to conventional diffusion generation may need adjustment when representation learning is a central goal.
icml-2024-denoising-autoregressive-repre.tldr: DARL combines autoregressive image-patch prediction with denoising to learn visual representations that approach leading masked prediction models under fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge from a teacher detector to a student requires deciding what information to transfer and how to compare it. These choices vary across detector architectures, detection paradigms, and label assignments, making manual design difficult. DetKDS automates the search for distillation policies for both similar and structurally different teacher-student pairs.

Its search space includes global image features, foreground and background features, instance features, classification responses, and localization responses. It also searches transformations, distance functions, and loss weights. To manage this large space, a divide-and-conquer evolutionary procedure first develops distillers for individual information sources, then optimizes how their losses are weighted together.

Experiments across several detectors show improvements over leading distillation methods in detection and instance segmentation. Reported gains over baseline detectors range from 3.5 to 4.1 AP across five named architectures. The search results also yield guidance for designing detection distillers. The broader contribution is a systematic way to adapt knowledge transfer to the particular teacher and student without requiring expert-designed policies or additional tuning.
icml-2024-detkds-knowledge-distillation-.tldr: DetKDS searches automatically for detector-specific knowledge distillation policies and reports gains in object detection and instance segmentation.

paragraphs: This paper introduces E-UC³RL for sequential decision problems whose dynamics and rewards depend on context. Its objective is to control regret, the accumulated performance shortfall over learning episodes. The method works with finite function classes representing context-dependent transitions and rewards, allowing the analysis to account for general function approximation.

The guarantees assume realizability and access to offline least-squares and log-loss regression oracles. Computational efficiency is conditional on those oracles being efficient. The regret bound grows with the square root of the number of episodes and includes dependence on the horizon, state and action counts, function-class sizes, and an Eluder dimension defined using Hellinger distance.

The Eluder dimension brings the structure of the transition function class into the learning guarantee. The authors identify their method, to their knowledge, as the first efficient, rate-optimal regret minimization algorithm in this general offline function approximation setting for contextual MDPs. They also extend Eluder dimension to general bounded metrics, providing a mathematical contribution beyond the particular algorithm.
icml-2024-eluder-based-regret-for-stocha.tldr: E-UC³RL gives a rate-optimal regret guarantee for contextual MDPs under realizability and is efficient when its offline regression oracles are efficient.

paragraphs: Evolving Subnetwork Training addresses the high computational cost of training large language models. Motivated by redundancy in their parameters, it trains sampled subnetworks whose size increases over time. This makes the amount of model computation used during training something that can evolve rather than remain fixed throughout the process.

The method samples subnetworks across model layers and within two common layer components: multi-head attention and multilayer perceptrons. Gradually increasing the sampled subnetworks' size reduces the training computation required. The authors also provide theoretical studies based on training dynamics and dropout theory to support the feasibility of this training approach.

Applied to GPT2 and TinyLlama, the method saves 26.7% and 25.0% of training FLOPs, respectively, without increasing loss on the pretraining dataset. It also improves performance on downstream tasks in the reported evaluations, suggesting a generalization benefit. These findings support evolving subnetwork size as a way to reduce training arithmetic while preserving the measured pretraining objective and improving subsequent task performance in the tested models.
icml-2024-evolving-subnetwork-training-f.tldr: Gradually enlarging sampled subnetworks reduces GPT2 and TinyLlama training FLOPs without increasing pretraining loss and improves evaluated downstream performance.

paragraphs: Protein language models learn from protein sequences before their representations or weights are reused for property and structure prediction. Although this transfer has been successful, it leaves a question about which learned features actually help downstream tasks. This paper investigates that relationship through a systematic analysis rather than treating pretraining quality as automatically equivalent to downstream usefulness.

The study includes 370 experiments varying downstream tasks, architectures, model sizes, model depths, and pretraining time. Almost all evaluated tasks benefit from pretrained models compared with naive sequence representations. For the majority of tasks, however, performance does not scale with pretraining and instead depends on low-level features acquired early in the pretraining process.

These observations distinguish the value of having pretrained features from the value of extending the existing pretraining approach. The results point to a mismatch between current protein-model pretraining paradigms and most applications examined. They motivate better pretraining methods that more directly support downstream needs, while preserving the finding that pretraining itself is beneficial for almost all studied tasks.
icml-2024-feature-reuse-and-scaling-unde.tldr: Across 370 experiments, most protein prediction tasks benefit from pretraining but rely mainly on early-learned features rather than improving as pretraining scales.

paragraphs: Explaining a generative language model requires accounting for more than a single predicted label. At each step, the model produces a distribution over vocabulary tokens with different semantic relationships, and it repeats this process across a generated sequence. These properties make attribution methods developed for discriminative language models poorly suited to faithful explanations of generation.

GiLOT uses optimal transport to assess how removing each input token changes the distribution of possible generated sequences. Its comparison accounts for token similarity, so changes between semantically related tokens can be treated differently from changes between dissimilar ones. The resulting distributional change provides an estimate of each input token's contribution to generation.

The authors evaluate GiLOT on Llama models and fine-tuned derivatives at multiple scales. Under fair comparison settings, it outperforms existing methods on several faithfulness metrics. The findings support evaluating input importance through changes in the structured distribution of generated outputs, with both semantic relationships and sequential generation included in the explanation method.
icml-2024-gilot-interpreting-generative-.tldr: GiLOT attributes language-model outputs to input tokens using optimal transport that accounts for semantic similarity and changes across generated sequences.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general-purpose gradient-guided nested sampling algorithm for posterior inference. The goal is to obtain useful samples from a posterior distribution while handling problems with substantial dimensionality and varied structure. Its main contribution is a combination of complementary computational techniques within one sampling approach.

GGNS brings together differentiable programming, Hamiltonian slice sampling, clustering, mode separation, dynamic nested sampling, and parallelization. The combination incorporates gradient information while also explicitly addressing separate modes of the distribution. The authors report that the resulting algorithm scales well with dimensionality and performs competitively across a collection of synthetic and real-world problems.

The paper also explores combining nested sampling with generative flow networks to produce large quantities of high-quality posterior samples. This combination yields faster discovery of modes and more accurate partition-function estimates in the reported work. Together, these results present an improved sampling algorithm and demonstrate the potential of connecting nested sampling with a learned generative mechanism for posterior inference.
icml-2024-improving-gradient-guided-nest.tldr: GGNS combines gradient-guided sampling techniques for competitive posterior inference and explores generative flow networks for faster mode discovery and better partition-function estimates.

paragraphs: Neural logic machines combine neural and symbolic structures for reasoning and decision-making. Although they can generalize well, their original training procedures can repeatedly produce similar mistakes, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper focuses on using those recurring failures as information that can guide subsequent training.

The proposed Failure Reflection Guided Regularizer first detects repeated mistakes and dynamically summarizes their root causes. It then penalizes the model when similar mistakes occur in later training iterations. This creates a feedback mechanism in which the model's history of failure shapes the regularization applied as learning continues.

The intended effect is to reduce repeated errors with similar causes and help training reach a better-performing solution more quickly. Experiments on multiple relational reasoning and decision-making tasks show improvements in performance, generalization, training efficiency, and data efficiency. These results support making recurring failure patterns an explicit part of the training objective, with benefits demonstrated across several aspects of learning in the evaluated neural logic machines.
icml-2024-improving-neural-logic-machine.tldr: A regularizer that identifies and penalizes recurring error causes improves neural logic machines' reasoning performance and learning efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Most existing safe reinforcement learning algorithms are based on optimization. This paper investigates whether a sampling-based approach can also produce useful performance with a safe policy. It introduces a Langevin policy that selects actions through a stochastic process, making the action-generation procedure itself central to the policy design.

The policy directly infers actions by numerically solving continuous-time Langevin dynamics over actions. To make this approach practical, the authors introduce Langevin Actor-Critic, or LAC, which accelerates policy inference. LAC collects transitions produced by the Langevin policy and uses a generator to reproduce them, connecting the original sampling process to a faster inference mechanism.

Experiments on MuJoCo-based tasks and Safety Gym show that LAC is effective and performs better than the alternatives evaluated. These results provide empirical support for sampling-based policy construction in safe reinforcement learning. The contribution combines a stochastic formulation for inferring actions with a practical method for reproducing its behavior, addressing both the policy idea and its computational use in reinforcement learning tasks.
icml-2024-langevin-policy-for-safe-reinf.tldr: Langevin Actor-Critic makes a sampling-based action policy practical and shows strong empirical performance on safe reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Few-shot action recognition requires adapting a pretrained model to new data using only a small number of labeled examples, often with a distribution shift. The central question is which parts of the pretrained knowledge should carry over. CDTD addresses this by identifying temporal dynamics intended to remain useful across domains.

The method uses causal representation learning during unsupervised pretraining to distinguish temporally invariant and variant representations. A later stage tunes the classifier with supervision. During adaptation, the transferable temporal dynamics remain fixed, while the image encoder and domain estimator are updated. This assigns different adaptation roles to the components of the model.

The approach assumes that domain information can be estimated well and that the pretrained temporal generation and transition models transfer well. Under this formulation, experiments show higher accuracy than leading alternatives across standard few-shot action recognition datasets. The findings support preserving reusable temporal structure while adapting components that connect new visual inputs and domain information to that structure.
icml-2024-learning-causal-domain-invaria.tldr: CDTD improves few-shot action recognition by preserving transferable temporal dynamics while adapting visual and domain components, assuming those dynamics and domain estimates transfer well.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection methods often assume that stored data can be revisited repeatedly. That assumption is awkward for streams, where observations arrive continuously and the process producing them can change. Even methods described as online may rely on periodic retraining to keep up. Online-iForest is designed explicitly around streaming conditions.

The method tracks the data-generating process as it evolves over time. This addresses adaptation as part of the streaming task itself, where both changing patterns and the speed of detection matter. The paper evaluates whether this design can maintain useful anomaly detection performance while improving the efficiency of processing ongoing data.

On real-world datasets, Online-iForest performs on par with online alternatives and closely approaches leading offline methods that are periodically retrained. It consistently surpasses the evaluated competitors in efficiency. The findings make it promising for settings where identifying unusual events quickly is especially valuable, including cybersecurity, fraud detection, and fault detection, while keeping the accuracy comparison distinct from its stronger efficiency result.
icml-2024-online-isolation-forest-65e2db.tldr: Online-iForest tracks evolving data streams with competitive anomaly detection performance and consistently better efficiency than the evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: Quantization compresses a model by converting its values to lower precision. Quantization-conditioned backdoors exploit this transformation: malicious behavior stays dormant in the full-precision model but becomes active after compression. This paper investigates why these backdoors appear and develops a defense for the resulting quantized model.

The authors observe that backdoor-related neurons change their activation distributions after quantization even on benign inputs. The shift is larger on poisoned inputs. This gives the defense a basis for comparing the compressed model with its full-precision version. The proposed method aligns their activations layer by layer to reduce the exposed backdoor behavior.

An additional module uses batch normalization statistics from the full-precision model to approximate poisoned activation distributions at each layer. This is designed to take advantage of the stronger shifts associated with poisoned samples. Extensive experiments support the defense's effectiveness. The key contribution is linking a measurable activation-distribution change to a corrective procedure, with the full-precision model serving as the reference for repairing the quantized model.
icml-2024-purifying-quantization-conditi.tldr: Aligning quantized-model activations with their full-precision counterparts provides an effective experimental defense against backdoors that activate after quantization.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across clients whose data can differ substantially, making generalization difficult. Some approaches try to improve generalization by using sharpness-aware minimization during each client's local training. Their aim is to find flatter minima, where the training objective is less sensitive to nearby changes in the model.

This paper identifies a mismatch between that local goal and the model produced by aggregation. Even when clients search for flat minima, the aggregated global model may not occupy a flat minimum of the global objective. The authors call this flatness discrepancy and analyze it theoretically to reconsider where the flatness objective should be applied.

They propose Federated Learning for Global Flatness, or FedGF, which explicitly seeks flatter minima for the global models. On heterogeneous federated learning benchmarks, the method reduces the discrepancy and produces substantial performance gains. The findings show why local flatness efforts alone can miss an important property of the final aggregated model, and support directly targeting global flatness in this setting.
icml-2024-rethinking-the-flat-minima-sea.tldr: FedGF targets flatness in the aggregated federated model, addressing a mismatch that persists despite clients' local flatness training.

paragraphs: Graph reconstruction requires turning latent embeddings into information about a graph. Inner-product decoders are a widely used framework for this step, but previous work has repeatedly observed limits in what they can represent. This paper focuses on explaining those limits theoretically, with sign rank providing the perspective identified in its title.

The central contribution is a theoretical account of a phenomenon that had already appeared across the literature. A representation-capacity question concerns which graph information the decoder can express through its chosen form. Establishing a mathematical explanation makes the decoder's structure a concrete part of understanding why graph reconstruction can be limited.

The authors also suggest straightforward modifications intended to circumvent the identified issue while retaining the inner-product framework. This gives the work both an explanatory and a design-oriented role: it connects observed reconstruction limitations to theory and points toward changes within the same broad family of decoders. The stated contribution concerns graph representation capacity and modifications to the decoding framework.
icml-2024-sign-rank-limitations-for-inne.tldr: The paper theoretically explains representation limits of inner-product graph decoders and proposes modifications that retain the inner-product framework.

paragraphs: Sliced-Wasserstein distance compares probability distributions by averaging Wasserstein distances between their one-dimensional projections. Computing it therefore involves averaging over directions on a sphere, a task naturally suited to Monte Carlo estimation. This paper improves that estimation by using spherical harmonics, a structured family of polynomial functions on the sphere.

The proposed Spherical Harmonics Control Variates method uses these functions as control variates in the Monte Carlo calculation. Their mathematical structure provides a way to improve the estimate of the spherical integral. The authors establish a better convergence rate than ordinary Monte Carlo for general measures, using a Lipschitz property of the sliced-Wasserstein integrand in the analysis.

They also prove a no-error property for Gaussian measures under a particular form of linear dependence between variables. That exactness is conditional on the stated Gaussian structure. Numerical experiments show better performance than leading methods for computing sliced-Wasserstein distance. The contribution combines general convergence improvements with a stronger special-case result and empirical evidence for more effective distance computation.
icml-2024-sliced-wasserstein-estimation-.tldr: Spherical-harmonic control variates improve sliced-Wasserstein estimation, with faster theoretical convergence and conditional exactness for certain Gaussian measures.

paragraphs: Continually learning from audio and video presents two connected difficulties. Meaningful relationships may occur only in limited spatial or temporal regions, and learning new material can overwrite previously acquired audiovisual relationships. STELLA addresses both by deciding which patches deserve attention during continual pretraining.

A multimodal encoder first scores patch importance, emphasizing audio and video patches that are semantically connected. A replay-guided correlation assessment then examines how current patches relate to earlier learning steps. It identifies patches with strong past correlations to help reduce corruption of previously learned knowledge as the model changes. These two assessments guide probabilistic patch selection.

Across multiple benchmarks, STELLA improves zero-shot retrieval compared with strong continual learning baselines while reducing memory consumption by approximately 45%. The results support selecting patches using both present cross-modal relevance and relationships to prior learning. This connects the method's two goals: concentrating training on useful audiovisual correspondences and protecting knowledge that could otherwise be overwritten during continued pretraining.
icml-2024-stella-continual-audio-video-p.tldr: STELLA selects informative audiovisual patches using current relevance and past correlations, improving continual retrieval performance while reducing memory use.

paragraphs: Ambiguous prediction tasks can have several plausible answers, so winner-takes-all learners produce a collection of hypotheses. Prior work connects their learned arrangement to centroidal Voronoi tessellations: the hypotheses are expected to organize themselves to quantize the shape of the conditional distribution optimally. This paper asks how that geometry can also support uncertainty estimation.

The authors construct a conditional density estimator using the geometric properties of the learned hypotheses. The original winner-takes-all training procedure stays unchanged. The contribution therefore concerns how to use the trained predictions to represent the distribution of possible outcomes, extending their role beyond providing a set of plausible answers.

The paper establishes theoretical advantages for both quantization and density estimation, then demonstrates competitive performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, including audio data. These results connect the spatial organization of predictions with a fuller description of uncertainty. They support extracting distributional information from winner-takes-all learners through an estimator designed around the geometry those learners already acquire.
icml-2024-winner-takes-all-learners-are-.tldr: A geometry-aware estimator turns winner-takes-all hypotheses into conditional density estimates without changing their original training procedure.
